elements.quote: A previous systematic review of the literature describing studies conducted in the Caribbean that presented the distribution of diabetes, its outcomes, and risk factors, by one or more social determinants, was updated to include sources from 1 January 2007 - 31 December 2016.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states that this work is an update of a previous systematic review, identifying the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: Objectives. To conduct an analysis of the most recent data on diabetes and its risk factors by gender and other social determinants of health to understand why its prevalence is higher among women than men in the Caribbean; to inform policy agenda-setting for diabetes prevention and control in the Caribbean; and to identify gaps in the evidence that require further research.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit statement of the main objectives/review questions.

elements.quote: Studies were ­ included if the complete text was available; if not, they were excluded. There were no limits regarding the language of publication. Diabetes outcomes and risk factors were considered among both the general population and those with diabetes.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies key inclusion and exclusion criteria (requirement of complete text, no language limits, types of outcomes/populations considered).

elements.quote: A previous systematic review ... was updated to include sources from 1 January 2007 - 31 December 2016. Surveys by the World Health Organization (WHO) were also included.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the date range searched and that WHO surveys were included, but does not list the specific bibliographic databases or give when each source was last searched.

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed using criteria applied by Brown and colleagues (14) for each relationship and classified as follows: Sample size ≥ 50 people
elements.reason: The abstract describes the method used to assess risk of bias (using criteria from Brown et al.) and indicates classification was applied.

elements.quote: Where data were sufficient, meta-analyses were undertaken.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies that meta-analyses were conducted to synthesize results when data permitted.

elements.quote: A total of 8 326 manuscripts were identified. Of those, 282 were selected for full text review, and 114, for abstraction. In all, 36 papers, including WHO-related surveys, had sufficient information for meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The abstract reports numbers of manuscripts screened and included (studies) and numbers used in meta-analysis, and summarizes some study types (WHO surveys), but does not report the total number of participants.

elements.quote: More women compared to men were obese (OR: 2.1; 95%CI = 1.65 - 2.69), physically inactive (OR: 2.18; 95%CI = 1.75 - 2.72), and had diabetes (OR: 1.48; 95%CI = 1.25 - 1.76). More men smoked (OR: 4.27; 95%CI = 3.18 - 5.74) and had inadequate fruit and vegetable intake (OR: 1.37; 95%CI = 1.21 - 1.57)
elements.reason: The abstract presents main outcome results (with effect estimates and CIs) but does not provide the number of included studies and participants for each reported outcome.

elements.quote: More women compared to men were obese (OR: 2.1; 95%CI = 1.65 - 2.69)... More men smoked (OR: 4.27; 95%CI = 3.18 - 5.74)
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports summary estimates (odds ratios) with 95% confidence intervals for main outcomes.

elements.quote: More women compared to men were obese ... More men smoked ...
elements.reason: When comparing groups (women versus men), the abstract indicates the direction of effect and which group had higher odds for each outcome.

The abstract does not include a brief summary of important limitations (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision); limitations are discussed elsewhere in the manuscript but are not in the abstract.

elements.quote: Conclusion. Thirty-six papers were added to the previously conducted systematic review; of those, 13 were added to the meta-analysis. Diabetes and its risk factors (primarily obesity and physical inactivity) continue to disproportionately affect women in the Caribbean. Smoking interventions should be targeted at men in this geographic area.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of findings and implications for policy and practice.
The abstract does not report the primary source of funding; funding is reported in the Conclusion/funding section of the paper but not in the abstract.
The abstract does not provide a registry name or registration number for the review.

elements.quote: Objectives. To conduct an analysis of the most recent data on diabetes and its risk factors by gender and other social determinants of health to understand why its prevalence is higher among women than men in the Caribbean; to inform policy agenda-setting for diabetes prevention and control in the Caribbean; and to identify gaps in the evidence that require further research.
elements.reason: The abstract contains an explicit statement of multiple review objectives (analysis of recent data by gender and social determinants; inform policy agenda-setting; identify evidence gaps), satisfying the requirement to state the review's objectives/questions.

elements.quote: This was a systematic review of diabetes distribution, risk factors, and outcomes, by social determinants of health, in the Caribbean.
elements.reason: The review addresses distribution, risk factors, and outcomes by social determinants rather than effects of interventions, so planned intervention comparisons using PICO are not applicable.

elements.quote: Caribbean study population Adult participants ( ≥ 18 years of age) when considering diabetes and its outcomes, or participants ≥ 12 years when considering risk factors Outcomes stratified by at least one of the social determinants Quantitative study design (observational/intervention) ... Sample size ≥ 50 people
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies study population (Caribbean), age inclusion thresholds (≥18 for outcomes, ≥12 for risk factors), required outcome stratification by social determinants, eligible study designs (quantitative observational/intervention), and a minimum sample size, fulfilling specification of study characteristics used to determine eligibility.

elements.quote: this review included sources from 1 January 2007 - 31 December 2016. ... Studies were ­ included if the complete text was available; if not, they were excluded. There were no limits regarding the language of publication.
elements.reason: The manuscript states the eligible publication years, that complete text availability was required (reports without full text excluded), and explicitly notes no language restrictions, addressing report characteristic eligibility.

elements.quote: Did not meet inclusion criteria: 218 —Did not meet age criteria: 7 —Did not describe an outcome of interest by one of the selected social determinants: 56 —Other reasons: 142 —Unable to retrieve full text: 13
elements.reason: The flowchart enumerates studies excluded for not describing an outcome of interest vs other reasons (including inability to retrieve full text), which partly distinguishes types of exclusion. However, it does not explicitly differentiate exclusion because an outcome was not measured versus exclusion because outcome results were not reported, so the distinction is incomplete.

elements.quote: Number of articlesa with sufficient detail for meta-analysis: 36 ... Diabetes prevalence 24   Obesity 20   Physical inactivity 15   Smoking 20
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies the groups used in syntheses (which outcomes were combined in meta-analyses and their article counts) and links these groups to the comparisons (e.g., diabetes prevalence, obesity, physical inactivity, smoking) used in the review.

elements.quote: Other social determinants were too heterogeneously defined to allow for meta-analysis; these were described narratively.
elements.reason: The manuscript gives a rationale for not meta-analysing certain social determinants (heterogeneous definitions) and explains that these were described narratively, but it does not consistently provide explicit rationales for other notable eligibility restrictions (e.g., age cutoffs, requirement for complete text) beyond procedural statements, so the explanation of all notable restrictions is only partially provided.

The manuscript reports an overall date range for included sources (1 January 2007 - 31 December 2016) but does not report the date on which each information source was last searched or consulted as required (no per-source search dates are provided).

elements.quote: A systematic search was conducted of PubMed Central (U.S. National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, Maryland, United States); EMBASE (Excerpta Medica Database, Elsevier, Amsterdam, the Netherlands); the Virtual Health Library, including LILACS (Latin American and Caribbean Center on Health Sciences Information, PAHO/WHO, São Paolo, Brazil; BIREME); MedCarib (Health sciences data from the English speaking Caribbean; BIREME); and IBECS (Biographic Index on Health Sciences; BIREME).
elements.reason: The names of multiple bibliographic databases searched are reported, but the manuscript does not report the search interface/platform details for each database (beyond organizational attributions) nor the available coverage dates for each database, so reporting is incomplete.

elements.quote: Reports from the WHO STEP-wise approach to noncommunicable disease risk factor surveillance surveys (STEPS; 7) and other nationally representative NCD reports were identified from PAHO (8) and WHO (9) websites.
elements.reason: Names of registers/repositories (WHO STEPS, PAHO, WHO) from which reports were identified are provided, but no information on any date restrictions or specific date ranges applied to those registers/repositories is reported.

elements.quote: Reports from the WHO STEP-wise approach to noncommunicable disease risk factor surveillance surveys (STEPS; 7) and other nationally representative NCD reports were identified from PAHO (8) and WHO (9) websites.
elements.reason: The manuscript names websites (PAHO and WHO) as online sources consulted, but it does not provide the URLs for these sites or for other online sources, so the requirement is only partly met.
There is no statement that organisations or manufacturers were contacted to identify studies, nor are any such organisations named as having been contacted.
The manuscript does not describe contacting any individuals (types of persons) to identify studies; no information about individuals contacted is provided.
The types of reference lists examined (e.g., reference lists of included studies, reviews, citation searching) are not specified in the provided evidence.
No information is provided about backward or forward citation searching (no seed reports, citation index/platform, or dates of such searches are reported).
The manuscript does not report consulting specific journals or conference proceedings with associated source names, dates covered, or search methods for these sources in the provided evidence.

No complete search strategies or exact search strings run for each database/register/website are reported in the provided evidence; only the names of databases searched and a reference to using the same search strategies as a prior review are given.

elements.quote: this review included data for three additional years (2014 - 2016), extending the collection from 1 January 2007 - 31 December 2016.
elements.reason: A date range limit is reported (1 Jan 2007–31 Dec 2016), but other search limits (e.g., language, study type filters) are not fully described or explicitly justified with eligibility criteria in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The study protocol for this review followed that of Sobers-­ Grannum and colleagues (4) and added newer data collected from NCD survey reports available on the websites of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) and WHO. In short, using the same search strategies as the original (4), this review included data for three additional years (2014 - 2016)...
elements.reason: The authors cite a published prior review/protocol (Sobers-Grannum et al.) as the search approach used and describe an adaptation (adding data from PAHO/WHO websites and extending the years covered).
No mention in the provided evidence of using natural-language processing or text-analysis tools to identify or refine search terms.
No information is provided about tools used to translate search strings between sources.
The provided evidence contains no description of any validation of the search strategy or validation studies/process.
There is no description in the supplied evidence of any peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) or the process used.

elements.quote: Guided by the Progress-plus checklist (6), the social determinants examined were: gender; marital status; income; housing; urban/rural location; Diaspora study population or other non-Caribbean
elements.reason: The authors describe the conceptual structure used to define the social determinants of interest (guided by the PROGRESS-Plus checklist) and list the final determinants examined, addressing the conceptual framing when not using PICO.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by two reviewers (LG and CB); conflicts were resolved by a third reviewer (NS). The full text of all retained articles was sought, and where available, was independently abstracted by two reviewers (LG and CB); again, any differences were resolved in discussion with a third reviewer (NS).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states two reviewers screened titles/abstracts and two reviewers independently abstracted full texts (LG and CB), with a third reviewer for conflicts.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by two reviewers (LG and CB); conflicts were resolved by a third reviewer (NS). The full text of all retained articles was sought, and where available, was independently abstracted by two reviewers (LG and CB); again, any differences were resolved in discussion with a third reviewer (NS).
elements.reason: The text explicitly states that screening and full-text abstraction were performed independently by two reviewers.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by two reviewers (LG and CB); conflicts were resolved by a third reviewer (NS). ... any differences were resolved in discussion with a third reviewer (NS).
elements.reason: The process for resolving disagreements is described: conflicts/differences were resolved by discussion with a third reviewer (NS).
No information is provided about contacting study investigators or processes to obtain/confirm eligibility information from investigators.
No methods for translating abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Bibliographic information for each study was entered into the Rayyan online data system (Qatar Computing Research Institute, Doha, Qatar; 10).
elements.reason: The manuscript names the Rayyan online data system used for bibliographic management/screening, but does not describe how any automation tools were integrated into the selection process or whether automation features were used.
No information about externally derived classifiers (versions/references), their role, or records removed before screening is provided.
No information about internally derived classifiers, their training, validation, or use is provided.
No description of machine-learning prioritisation tools or stopping/prioritisation rules is provided in the evidence.
No mention of crowdsourcing platforms or their integration into study selection is present in the provided text.

elements.quote: Duplicates excluded by hand: 308
elements.reason: While the flowchart shows duplicates excluded manually, there is no description of previously screened datasets used to eliminate records or how such datasets were derived; thus this conditional item is not reported.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by two reviewers (LG and CB); conflicts were resolved by a third reviewer (NS). The full text of all retained articles was sought, and where available, was independently abstracted by two reviewers (LG and CB); again, any differences were resolved in discussion with a third reviewer (NS).
elements.reason: States that two reviewers (LG and CB) performed independent abstraction of full texts (and titles/abstracts), specifying the number of reviewers collecting data from each report.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by two reviewers (LG and CB); conflicts were resolved by a third reviewer (NS). The full text of all retained articles was sought, and where available, was independently abstracted by two reviewers (LG and CB); again, any differences were resolved in discussion with a third reviewer (NS).
elements.reason: Explicitly reports that multiple data collectors (two reviewers) worked independently for screening and for data abstraction.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by two reviewers (LG and CB); conflicts were resolved by a third reviewer (NS). The full text of all retained articles was sought, and where available, was independently abstracted by two reviewers (LG and CB); again, any differences were resolved in discussion with a third reviewer (NS).
elements.reason: Describes the process for resolving disagreements: conflicts or differences were resolved by discussion with a third reviewer (NS).
No text in the provided evidence describes processes used to obtain or confirm data from study investigators.

elements.quote: Bibliographic information for each study was entered into the Rayyan online data system (Qatar Computing Research Institute, Doha, Qatar; 10). A form for data abstraction was designed using OpenOffice™ Base (Oracle Corporation, Santa Clara, California, United States).
elements.reason: Mentions use of Rayyan for bibliographic information and an OpenOffice Base abstraction form, but does not describe automation tools used specifically for data collection, nor details on their use, training, or validation; thus partially addresses automation/software but lacks required details.
No methods for translating articles or how non-English articles were handled are reported in the provided evidence (only that there were no language limits).
No software or methods for extracting data from figures are specified in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: It was possible to have more than one paper published for a study.
elements.reason: While the text notes that more than one paper could be published for a study, there is no description of decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or resolving inconsistencies between them.

elements.quote: For the general population, the review looked at: obesity, including measures of body mass index (BMI), waist circumference (WC), and abdominal obesity; physical inactivity; tobacco use; measures of diet quality, e.g., consumption of fruits and vegetables, diet quality scores, etc.; and type 1 and type 2 diabetes prevalence and incidence. Among those with diabetes, the review considered: control measures, including glucose, glycated hemoglobin, blood pressure, and lipids; measures of incidence or prevalence of retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, diabetic foot, and lower extremity amputation; and mortality.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists multiple outcome domains for both the general population and people with diabetes and provides definitions/measure types (e.g., BMI, WC, abdominal obesity, physical inactivity, glucose, HbA1c, etc.).

No explicit specification of the time frame of measurement for each outcome domain (e.g., time points or measurement windows for outcomes) is reported in the provided evidence. Only the review search years (2007–2016) are given, not measurement time frames for outcomes.
There is no explicit statement saying whether all results compatible with each outcome domain (for all measures, time points, analyses) were sought.

elements.quote: Only population-based, cross-­ sectional studies that measured the outcomes as dichotomous variables were included for meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The methods describe a selection process used when assembling results for meta-analysis (restricting to population-based cross-sectional studies with dichotomous outcome measurement), i.e. how results were selected within outcome domains for meta-analysis.
No changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance are reported in the provided evidence, so reporting of such changes with rationales does not apply.
No changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains are reported in the provided evidence, so reporting of such changes with rationales does not apply.
The manuscript does not explicitly state which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting conclusions nor provide a rationale for prioritisation.

elements.quote: For the general population, the review looked at: obesity, including measures of body mass index (BMI), waist circumference (WC), and abdominal obesity; physical inactivity; tobacco use; measures of diet quality, e.g., consumption of fruits and vegetables, diet quality scores, etc.; and type 1 and type 2 diabetes prevalence and incidence. Among those with diabetes, the review considered: control measures, including glucose, glycated hemoglobin, blood pressure, and lipids; measures of incidence or prevalence of retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, diabetic foot, and lower extremity amputation; and mortality.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the other variables (outcomes and measures) sought and, in some cases, specifies measurement types (e.g., BMI, WC, abdominal obesity), indicating these variables were defined/identified for data collection.

elements.quote: Limitations. A major limitation of this review was the poor data quality and study reports. Of the total articles, 60% were classified as having a high or moderate risk of bias, with a lack of adjustment for age and other confounders being the largest contributing factor(s). Also, a large proportion of articles lacked detailed descriptions of methodology and outcomes, participant selection, measurement, and confounding. Many had missing data.
elements.reason: The text describes that many studies had missing or unclear information and notes this as a limitation, but it does not describe any specific assumptions made about missing or unclear study information or how such missingness was handled or imputed during data extraction.

elements.quote: Guided by the Progress-plus checklist (6), the social determinants examined were: gender; marital status; income; housing; urban/rural location; Diaspora study population or other non-Caribbean
elements.reason: The manuscript cites the Progress-plus checklist as guiding which social determinant data items to examine. Additionally, the data abstraction form is said to be guided by the STROBE statement and PRISMA (text_2), indicating cited tools were used to determine data items.

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed using criteria applied by Brown and colleagues (14) for each relationship and classified as follows:
elements.reason: The manuscript cites the criteria applied by Brown et al. as the basis for risk-of-bias assessment, but does not name a specific risk-of-bias tool (with a formal tool name) or provide a version identifier. Thus the tool source is referenced but a clear tool name/version is not specified.

elements.quote: Low risk of bias (all criteria are met)-response rate > 75%, missing data < 10%, full description of sampling strategy, adjustment of measures by age and other potential confounders (such as sex or ethnicity), as appropriate, and objective measurement of disease measures; Medium risk of bias (one or more criterion)-response rate 50% - 75%, missing data 10% - 15%, adjustment of measures by age and other potential confounders (such as sex or ethnicity), as appropriate, and subjective measurement of disease measures; High risk of bias (one or more criterion)-response rate ≤ 50%, missing data > 15%, inappropriate adjustment for confounders (i.e., missing important adjustment or no adjustment), poor sampling strategy, inappropriate assessment of the disease measure; Unclear-not enough information to make an assessment.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly specifies the domains/criteria used to assess risk of bias (response rate, amount of missing data, sampling strategy, adjustment for confounders, objective vs subjective measurement) and provides thresholds for low/medium/high/unclear ratings.

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed using criteria applied by Brown and colleagues (14) for each relationship and classified as follows: ... Low risk of bias (all criteria are met)-response rate > 75%... Medium risk of bias ... High risk of bias ... Unclear-not enough information to make an assessment. Overall relationship quality from risk of bias was as follows: high risk ( n = 98), medium risk ( n = 127), low risk ( n = 68), and unclear ( n = 81).
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias judgement was made (categories low/medium/high/unclear) and the rules/thresholds used to derive these categories are reported; overall counts of relationships in each category are provided.
No evidence in the supplied text that any adaptations to an existing risk-of-bias tool were described.
No evidence that a newly developed risk-of-bias tool was created or described; no public accessibility information is provided.

elements.quote: Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by two reviewers (LG and CB); conflicts were resolved by a third reviewer (NS). The full text of all retained articles was sought, and where available, was independently abstracted by two reviewers (LG and CB); again, any differences were resolved in discussion with a third reviewer (NS).
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the number of reviewers and independence for screening and data abstraction (two reviewers, with a third resolving conflicts). However, it does not explicitly state how many reviewers assessed risk of bias specifically or the procedures for resolving disagreements in the risk-of-bias assessment itself.
No information is provided about contacting study investigators or processes used to obtain/confirm risk-of-bias information from study authors.
There is no evidence that automation tools were used for risk-of-bias assessment nor any description of their use, training, performance, or validation.

elements.quote: En comparación con los hombres, un mayor número de mujeres eran obesas (razón de posibilidades [OR]: 2,1; IC de 95% = 1,65 - 2,69), físicamente inactivas (OR: 2,18; IC de 95% = 1,75 - 2,72) y tenían diabetes (OR: 1,48; IC de 95% = 1,25 - 1,76). Un mayor número de hombres eran fumadores (OR: 4,27; IC de 95% = 3,18 - 5,74) y presentaban un consumo insuficiente de frutas y verduras (OR: = 1,37; IC de 95% = 1,21 - 1,57).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports odds ratios (OR) with 95% CIs for multiple outcomes (obesity, physical inactivity, diabetes, smoking, insufficient fruit/vegetable intake), specifying the effect measure used for those outcomes.
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect sizes (e.g., what constitutes small/medium/large effects) or a rationale for such thresholds are reported in the provided evidence.
No methods describing re-expression of synthesized results using another effect measure (e.g., converting OR to risk ratio or to mean difference) are presented in the retrieved text.

elements.quote: Only population-based, cross-­ sectional studies that measured the outcomes as dichotomous variables were included for meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The manuscript justifies the choice of effect measure indirectly by stating that included outcomes for meta-analysis were measured as dichotomous variables, supporting the use of ratio measures (here, odds ratios) in synthesis.

elements.quote: Only population-based, cross-­ sectional studies that measured the outcomes as dichotomous variables were included for meta-analysis. ... Measures were included in the narrative review when at least four relationships from multiple studies were available. Other social determinants were too heterogeneously defined to allow for meta-analysis; these were described narratively.
elements.reason: The Methods section explicitly states the decision rules for which studies were eligible for the meta-analyses (population-based, cross-sectional, dichotomous outcomes) and the criterion for inclusion in the narrative synthesis (at least four relationships from multiple studies); it also notes that heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis for other determinants.

elements.quote: Only population-based, cross-­ sectional studies that measured the outcomes as dichotomous variables were included for meta-analysis. Meta-analyses were conducted and random effects models were fitted... elements.quote: Limitations. A major limitation of this review was the poor data quality and study reports. Of the total articles, 60% were classified as having a high or moderate risk of bias, with a lack of adjustment for age and other confounders being the largest contributing factor(s). Also, a large proportion of articles lacked detailed descriptions of methodology and outcomes, participant selection, measurement, and confounding. Many had missing data. These issues contributed to > 20% of papers being classified as having an 'unclear' risk of bias. Other systematic reviews of non-randomized evidence in the Caribbean have also reported large proportions with a high risk of bias (14, 48). This speaks to the quality of reporting in the region and the necessity for establishing and adopting reporting standards to improve output. Despite the wide scope of this systematic review, heterogeneous definitions of social determinants (especially education levels, income groups, and measures of socioeconomic status) and outcome measures made it impossible to conduct meta-analyses beyond gender.

elements.quote: Despite the wide scope of this systematic review, heterogeneous definitions of social determinants (especially education levels, income groups, and measures of socioeconomic status) and outcome measures made it impossible to conduct meta-analyses beyond gender. ... The WHO STEPwise approach is an example of a standardized methodology that collects several social determinants data in a systematic way (e.g., gender, age, marital status, education, and income) across many countries (7). However, typically STEPS surveys are too small to have sufficient statistical power for meaningful sub-group analyses by social determinant, tending instead to provide precise estimates of prevalence for men, women, and age groups combined. The methodology does not provide sufficient statistical power for stratification by other indicators at the country level. Alternatively, existing sources could be pooled to add statistical power and enable regional estimates of other social determinants by outcome. If leading organizations, such as WHO and PAHO, were to promote the use of standardized, operational definitions of social determinant indicators, they could facilitate more robust and comparable research of health inequalities.
